summary:
Karaman is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework. No Karaman-specific statute, police action, incident or court case appears in the sources behind this record, so what a trans visitor faces in the province is set by country-wide law and enforcement practice rather than by any local instrument.

The most consequential instrument is a leaked omnibus draft, the "11th Judicial Package", reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' imprisonment, and to punish participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, and would require documented permanent infertility plus repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals carrying out such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns that it would drive treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention. The release describes a draft, not enacted law.

Kaos GL's 2025 review finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy across the country. Instructions framing a "Year of the Family" were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association was closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned. The monitoring recorded roughly 313 violations overall, about two and a half times the previous year, alongside 299 detention decisions. Six right-to-life violations were recorded, three of them hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Torture and ill-treatment violations rose to 89 from 51, and freedom-of-expression violations rose from 216 to 540.

Street-level checks are how that posture reaches a visitor on the ground. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that no fines were issued but that the police documented them anyway, and that enforcement was being applied to her before any new law had passed. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk wherever appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

The document rule itself carries a penalty. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Every checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration runs on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is running ahead of legislation. The 11th Judicial Package remained a draft when Human Rights Watch reported it, yet trans women stopped in Istanbul in 2025 described being documented under measures whose statute had not been passed, which indicates that pending provisions shape police behaviour before they carry the force of law.

The regime's depth predates the current government's instruments. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence rather than as a statement of current law.

There is a standing conflict between Turkish practice and the regional human-rights framework it is party to: the legal experts cited on the Istanbul GBT checks place them in breach of Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects liberty and security of person. No court ruling against the practice is reported in these sources.

Where a comparison is useful, the pattern of a state apparatus formalising hostility is visible across monitoring and litigation channels at once: Kaos GL's tallies, the international organisations' reporting, and opposition parliamentary interventions all describe the same period, 2024 to 2025, from different directions.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this record concerns Karaman province itself. Nothing local is documented: no provincial statute, no police directive, no incident, no court file, and no reporting on facilities, Pride events or detention practice in Karaman. The province's entry is an application of national material and should be read that way.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted, amended or withdrawn after 29 October 2025 is unresolved in these sources; only its status as a leaked draft at the time of reporting is established.

Whether GBT street checks of the kind documented in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district are carried out in Karaman, and with what frequency, is not sourced. The claim that foreign visitors must produce original identification at checkpoints is stated at national level with a stated fine of up to 3,000 Turkish lira, but no Karaman-specific checkpoint data is available.

The cause of death of the transgender prisoner at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 remains unresolved in these sources. Rights groups demanded an independent investigation and reported delayed medical response, delayed forensic entry and untaken witness statements, but no finding, charge or verdict is recorded here.
